questions.title: Read a logarithm as a power
questions.prompt_html:
The logarithm has base \(4\).

Find \(\log_{4}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\) exactly.
questions.solution_html:
Write the base as \(2^{2}\) and its argument as \(2^{-2}\). If the logarithm is \(x\), then \(2^{2x}=2^{-2}\).

Equate the exponents: \(2x=-2\) and hence \(x=-1\).

\(-1\)
questions.hint_html: Relate the two powers using one common base.

questions.title: Find an unknown logarithm base
questions.prompt_html:
The base \(b\) is positive and differs from \(1\). The equation is \(\log_{b}\left(4\right)=2\).

Find \(b\).
questions.solution_html:
Change to exponential form: \(b^{2}=4\).

Let \(D=3\log_{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-\log_{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\).

  1. Evaluate D exactly.

    [2]

  2. Write \(2^D\) as a rational number.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Since \(2^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(2^{-2}=\frac{1}{4}\), the logarithms are \(-1\) and \(-2\).

Apply the coefficient to the first logarithm only: \(D=3\cdot(-1)-(-2)=-1\).

\(-1\)

(b) \(2^{-1}=\frac{1}{2^{1}}=\frac{1}{2}\). The negative exponent gives the reciprocal.

\(\frac{1}{2}\)
questions.hint_html: Find the two exponents before applying the coefficient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the two exponents before applying the coefficient.
Substitute the exponent from (a) and apply the index laws.

questions.solution_html:

Apply the coefficient to the first logarithm only: \(D=2\cdot(2)-(1)=3\).

\(3\)

(b) \(2^{3}=8\). Multiply the base by itself as indicated by the exponent.

\(8\)

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the two exponents before applying the coefficient.

questions.title: Use the quotient law before evaluating
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(L=\log_{2}\left(8\right)-\log_{2}\left(2\right)\).

  1. Evaluate L exactly.

    [2]

  2. Write \(\log_{2}\left(2\right)+L\) as one logarithm to base \(2\).

questions.solution_html:

Because \(2^{2}=4\), the logarithm equals \(2\).

\(2\)

(b) Use \(L=\log_{2}\left(4\right)\). The sum multiplies the two arguments, so the combined argument is \(2\cdot 4=8\).

\(\log_{2}\left(8\right)\)

questions.title: Combine three logarithms into one
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x>0\), the expression is \(3\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\log_{2}\left(2\right)-\log_{2}\left(4\right)\).

  1. Write this expression as a single logarithm.

    [2]

  2. Solve when the expression equals \(\log_{2}\left(4\right)\). Give the exact solution.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Move the outside coefficient into the argument: \(3\log_{2}\left(x\right)=\log_{2}\left(x^3\right)\).

The sum and difference multiply by \(2\) and divide by \(4\). This gives \(\log_{2}\left(\frac{2x^3}{4}\right)=\log_{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}x^3\right)\).

\(\log_{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}x^3\right)\)

(b) Since the bases agree, set the arguments equal: \(\frac{1}{2}x^3=4\).

Divide by \(\frac{1}{2}\) and take the positive cube root of \(8\). The original domain is \(x>0\).

\(x=2\)
questions.hint_html: Use the power, product and quotient laws.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the power, product and quotient laws.
Equate the arguments and keep the positive solution.

Let \(L=\log_{2}\left(48\right)-\log_{2}\left(3\right)\).

  1. Evaluate L exactly.

    [2]

  2. Write \(\log_{2}\left(3\right)+L\) as one logarithm to base \(2\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The same-base difference is \(\log_{2}\left(\frac{48}{3}\right)\). The quotient is \(16\).

Because \(2^{4}=16\), the logarithm equals \(4\).

\(4\)

(b) Use \(L=\log_{2}\left(16\right)\). The sum multiplies the two arguments, so the combined argument is \(3\cdot 16=48\).

\(\log_{2}\left(48\right)\)

questions.title: Combine three logarithms into one
questions.prompt_html:
For \(x>0\), the expression is \(2\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\log_{2}\left(4\right)-\log_{2}\left(3\right)\).

  1. Write this expression as a single logarithm.

    [2]

  2. Solve when the expression equals \(\log_{2}\left(3\right)\). Give the exact solution.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Move the outside coefficient into the argument: \(2\log_{2}\left(x\right)=\log_{2}\left(x^2\right)\).

The sum and difference multiply by \(4\) and divide by \(3\). This gives \(\log_{2}\left(\frac{4x^2}{3}\right)=\log_{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}x^2\right)\).

\(\log_{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}x^2\right)\)

(b) Since the bases agree, set the arguments equal: \(\frac{4}{3}x^2=3\).

Divide by \(\frac{4}{3}\) and take the positive square root of \(\frac{9}{4}\). The original domain is \(x>0\).

\(x=\frac{3}{2}\)

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the power, product and quotient laws.

questions.title: Choose a shared base to compare two logarithms

\(2\)

questions.title: Recover the scale and multiplier
questions.prompt_html:
A measurement is modelled by \(G(t)=Ab^t\), where \(A,b>0\). It is \(12\) at time \(1\) and \(3\) at time \(3\).

Find the exact multiplier \(b\).
questions.solution_html:
Write \(Ab^{1}=12\) and \(Ab^{3}=3\). Divide the later reading by the earlier to cancel \(A\).

The time gap is \(3-1=2\), so \(b^{2}=\frac{1}{4}\). Taking the positive root gives \(b=\frac{1}{2}\).

The multiplier describes decay.

\(\frac{1}{2}\)

questions.title: Find when an exponential decay model reaches a threshold
questions.prompt_html:

Divide the target reading by \(10\): \(e^{-\frac{1}{2}t}=\frac{1}{2}\).

Take logs before dividing by the negative rate: \(-\frac{1}{2}t=\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\). Therefore \(t=\frac{\ln(2)}{\frac{1}{2}}\).

Multiply the last reading by \(\frac{2}{3}\) to go forward one step: \(G(4)=\frac{32}{3}\cdot \frac{2}{3}=\frac{64}{9}\).

\(A=36,\qquad G(4)=\frac{64}{9}\)

questions.title: Find when an exponential decay model reaches a threshold
questions.prompt_html:
A sensor gives a reading of \(R=20e^{-\frac{1}{3}t}\) units after \(t\) hours, where \(t\geq0\). The alert level is \(5\).

  1. Find when the reading reaches the alert level. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [2]

  2. Explain why this is the only non-negative time when the alert level is met.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(4.159\text{ h}\)

(b) The reading decreases continuously from \(20\) towards \(0\) and crosses \(5\) once.
questions.solution_html:
(a) Divide the target reading by \(20\): \(e^{-\frac{1}{3}t}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Take logs before dividing by the negative rate: \(-\frac{1}{3}t=\ln\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\). Therefore \(t=\frac{\ln(4)}{\frac{1}{3}}\).

\(4.159\text{ h}\)

(b) The coefficient of \(t\) in the exponent is negative, so the positive exponential term decreases strictly to zero.

The alert level is between the starting value and the limiting value: \(0<5<20\).

The reading decreases continuously from \(20\) towards \(0\) and crosses \(5\) once.

questions.title: Find when an exponential decay model reaches a threshold
questions.prompt_html:
A sensor gives a reading of \(R=5+24e^{-\frac{2}{5}t}\) units after \(t\) hours, where \(t\geq0\). The alert level is \(8\).

  1. Find when the reading reaches the alert level. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [2]

  2. Explain why this is the only non-negative time when the alert level is met.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(5.199\text{ h}\)

(b) The reading decreases continuously from \(29\) towards \(5\) and crosses \(8\) once.
questions.solution_html:
(a) At the alert level, first subtract the background reading: \(8-5=3\).

Divide the amount above the background by \(24\): \(e^{-\frac{2}{5}t}=\frac{1}{8}\).

Take logs before dividing by the negative rate: \(-\frac{2}{5}t=\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)\). Therefore \(t=\frac{\ln(8)}{\frac{2}{5}}\).

\(5.199\text{ h}\)

(b) The coefficient of \(t\) in the exponent is negative, so the positive exponential term decreases strictly to zero.

The alert level is between the starting value and the limiting value: \(5<8<29\).

The reading decreases continuously from \(29\) towards \(5\) and crosses \(8\) once.
questions.hint_html: Isolate the exponential and solve by taking natural logarithms.

marking_criteria.description_html: Isolate the exponential and solve by taking natural logarithms.
Use the start value, limiting value and strict decrease.
